client: I've been really stressed lately because my partner keeps bringing up how I'm never around anymore, and I can tell they're getting fed up with it. I've been working late almost every night for the past few months, and every time I come home, there's this tension in the air that just makes everything feel worse. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, because the real problem is the job situation, and I don't see how that's going to fix itself.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a real heaviness right now — caught between the demands of work and the strain it's putting on your relationship, with little room to breathe. I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, and that's actually worth exploring, because sometimes when we feel stuck, our mind convinces us that *nothing* can shift — even the things that are within our reach. What do you think would feel like even a small step forward, if you let yourself imagine one?

client: I guess if I'm honest, the thing that feels most suffocating right now is that my partner and I barely talk anymore — like we're just coexisting in the same space, and I don't even know how to start that conversation without it turning into a fight. A small step forward... I don't know, maybe just saying something real to them instead of the usual surface stuff? But even imagining that makes me anxious, because what if I open up and it just makes things worse between us.
therapist: That fear of opening up and making things worse is so understandable — it can feel safer to stay on the surface than to risk a conversation that might spiral. But it's worth gently noticing that the "safe" silence is already causing pain, so part of you clearly senses that something real needs to be said. What do you imagine you'd most want your partner to *understand* about what you've been going through, if you knew they'd truly hear you?

client: I guess... I'd want them to understand that I'm not just being distant or cold, that there's actually a lot going on inside me that I don't even fully understand myself. Like, I'm not pulling away because I don't care — it's more like I'm drowning and I don't know how to ask for a life jacket without making them feel like they're the reason I'm drowning. But even just saying that out loud feels terrifying, because what if they take it the wrong way and it becomes this whole thing where I end up comforting them instead of actually getting what I need?
therapist: What you just said — about drowning and not wanting them to feel like the cause — is actually incredibly articulate and tender, and it tells me you have more clarity about your inner world than you're giving yourself credit for. That worry about ending up as the comforter instead of the one being heard is a really important pattern to notice, because it might be quietly stopping you from letting yourself be vulnerable even when you desperately need to be. What do you think gets in the way of you believing you deserve to have your needs heard in this relationship?

client: I guess... part of me doesn't really believe I do deserve it, if I'm being honest. Like, they have their own stuff going on, and who am I to add more weight to that? It's almost like I've convinced myself that being low-maintenance is the price I pay for keeping people around.
therapist: That belief — that you have to make yourself small to stay lovable — is such a painful way to move through a relationship, and it makes so much sense that it's left you feeling isolated. It's worth gently questioning where that idea actually came from, because it sounds less like a truth about you and more like a rule you learned somewhere along the way to feel safe. When you think back, does this sense of needing to be "low-maintenance" to keep people around feel familiar from earlier in your life?

client: Yeah, it does feel familiar, actually. I think back to when I was a kid and my mom was always so stressed and overwhelmed, and I just learned early on that asking for things or having needs made everything worse. So I kind of trained myself to be quiet and easy, and I guess I never really stopped doing that even as I got older.
therapist: That's a really profound connection you've just made — the quiet, self-sufficient child who learned that having needs created problems has grown into an adult who still carries that same rule, even in a relationship where you genuinely want closeness. What you learned back then was a way of surviving a stressful environment, and it made sense at the time, but it's worth asking whether that old rule is actually protecting you now or whether it's become the very thing keeping you from the connection you're longing for. What does it feel like to consider that your needs in this relationship might actually be valid and worth expressing, not a burden?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, there's a part of me that wants to believe it... but then another part just kind of shuts down and thinks, "yeah, but what if I actually am too much?" Like, intellectually I can hear what you're saying about the old rule not serving me anymore, but it doesn't really feel true in my body yet. It's like I know the words, but I can't quite make myself trust them.
therapist: That gap between knowing something in your head and feeling it in your body is so real, and it's actually one of the most honest things you can say about how change works — it's rarely a single moment of clarity, it's more like slowly building evidence that rewrites the old story. The thought "what if I'm too much" has had decades of practice, so it makes sense it doesn't dissolve just because we've named it. What's one moment, even a small one, where someone in your life responded to your needs with care rather than overwhelm — something that might serve as a tiny piece of counter-evidence to that old belief?

client: I mean... there was this one time a few months ago when I texted my friend Maya at like 11pm because I was spiraling pretty bad, and instead of just sending a quick "you okay?" she actually called me and stayed on the phone for almost an hour. I remember feeling so guilty the whole time, like I kept saying "I'm sorry, you should go to sleep" and she just kept saying "stop apologizing, I'm here because I want to be." But even now, telling you that, part of me is like... maybe she just felt obligated, maybe she was secretly annoyed and just didn't show it. It's hard to just take it at face value.
therapist: Maya stayed on the phone for an hour at 11pm and kept telling you to stop apologizing — and your mind's response is to find a way to make that care feel unsafe by questioning her motives. That's the old belief doing its job, protecting itself by discrediting the very evidence that challenges it. It's worth sitting with the fact that your mind does this *every time* — so the question isn't really about Maya's intentions, it's about what it would mean for you if you actually let yourself believe she wanted to be there. What do you think you'd have to give up if you accepted that you're not too much?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. Because I think... if I accepted that, I'd have to give up the excuse. Like, if I'm not too much, then I can't keep using that as the reason to stay distant or to preemptively pull away before people leave. And that's terrifying because then I'd actually have to be present in the friendship, really present, and risk getting hurt without any kind of protective story to fall back on.
therapist: What you just named takes real courage — recognizing that the "I'm too much" story, as painful as it is, has also been a kind of armor that keeps you from having to fully show up and risk being hurt. There's something bittersweet in that realization, because it means the belief isn't just a wound, it's also been a way of feeling in control. What would it feel like to experiment with being a little more present — maybe first with Maya, where you already have evidence of her care — and see what actually happens when you let someone in without the armor?

client: That word "armor" really hit me, because I think you're right, and I hate that you're right. Like, if I keep telling myself I'm too much, then I never have to actually find out if Maya would pull away, and that feels safer somehow. But the idea of just... letting her see more of me without that buffer is honestly terrifying, because what if I do it and she confirms my worst fear?
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — the armor has felt like the only thing standing between you and the most painful confirmation of that old belief. But it's worth noticing that right now, you're essentially choosing a guaranteed loneliness over a *possible* rejection, and part of you is starting to see that the certainty of staying hidden might actually cost more than the risk of being seen. What do you think one small, manageable moment of "letting Maya in" might look like — something real but not so big that it feels like stepping off a cliff?

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, part of me does recognize that the loneliness is already here, it's not like I'm avoiding pain by keeping the walls up. But when I try to think of something small with Maya, my mind just goes blank or immediately jumps to worst-case scenarios, like even something tiny will somehow open a door I won't be able to close again. I guess maybe... texting her back when she checks in, instead of leaving it on read for three days, but even saying that out loud makes my chest tighten.
therapist: That chest tightening when you imagine texting Maya back is your nervous system treating a simple text like a genuine threat — which tells you just how deeply that old protective pattern is wired in. But notice what you did just now: your mind went blank, then jumped to worst-case scenarios, and *then* found something small and real anyway, which means part of you is already pushing gently against the armor. Texting Maya back when she checks in is actually a perfect place to start — small enough to feel survivable, but real enough to begin collecting new evidence. What do you think you might say to her, even just a few words, that would feel honest without feeling like too much all at once?
